For (2) to hold, it is sufficient that  $ |U_t(0)| $ have the same continuous distribution at every date  $ t $. Continuity may be plausible when groups are aggregate entities (e.g., states or regions) and  $ Y_{g,t}(0) $ averages outcomes across many units. Importantly, (2) does not imply the usual parallel-trends condition. Provided  $ U_t(0) $ is integrable, parallel trends requires  $ \mathbb{E}[U_t(0)] = 0 $ at every date  $ t $. In contrast, (2) restricts only the distribution of  $ |U_t(0)| $ and places no restriction on the time evolution of the sign of  $ U_t(0) $. Consequently,  $ \mathbb{E}[U_t(0)] $ may be nonzero, may vary over time, and may change sign. The restriction is nevertheless substantive: it requires the entire distribution of the magnitude  $ |U_t(0)| $, including its tail behavior and all its quantiles, to remain stable over time.
